claims.text: Layered cuprate superconductors can exhibit high-temperature superconductivity.
The electronic structure of CuO2 planes fosters electron pairing.
Electron pairing in layered cuprates is mediated by spin fluctuations.
La2-xSrxCuO4 has a layered perovskite structure containing copper-oxide planes.
Substitution of La by Sr can optimally dope the cuprate.
Optimal Sr doping followed by cooling below the critical temperature enables superconductivity.
Some cuprates have critical temperatures in the range of 30–40 K.
High crystalline quality and controlled oxygen content are conditions for the proposed superconducting behavior.
The layered CuO2-plane structure provides the basis for strong electronic correlations.
The layered CuO2-plane structure provides the basis for spin-fluctuation-mediated pairing.
Spin fluctuations in the CuO2 planes act as the pairing glue for electrons.
Spin-fluctuation-mediated pairing overcomes Coulomb repulsion and enables Cooper-pair formation.
Cooper-pair formation produces superconductivity at temperatures elevated relative to conventional superconductors.
The doped cuprate will exhibit a measurable zero-resistance state below its critical temperature.
Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and neutron scattering will show evidence associated with spin-fluctuation-related pairing.
Undoped or lightly doped cuprates do not exhibit superconductivity and are typically insulating or non-superconducting metallic materials.
Variations in lattice structure, doping level, or defects can alter cuprate superconducting properties.
The proposed spin-fluctuation mechanism may not transfer directly to non-cuprate superconductors.
The roles of CuO2 planes and spin fluctuations are widely proposed but remain mechanistically uncertain and may differ among cuprate compounds.
